title: A living hope (1 Peter 1:3–9)
hook: born again into a living hope through the resurrection

segments.voice: Yesterday, James and the oil of the sick. Your line was the prayer of faith. Who did you let know they were held in mind? Day six hundred eight.

In Luke's Gospel, Peter warms himself at a fire in a courtyard and says, three times, that he doesn't know Jesus. Then a rooster crows, and he goes out and weeps. Years later the same man, now a leader of the Church, writes to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey, people being mocked and pushed to the edges for their faith. He could open with anything. A warning. A plan. A word about his own failures. Instead, after a short greeting, the first thing out of his pen is a blessing, and the blessing is about hope.
screen: `PETER BY THE COURTYARD FIRE.` → `YEARS LATER, A LETTER.` → `IT OPENS WITH HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy hath regenerated us unto a lively hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." Lively. In older English that word meant living. The Greek says it plainly: a living hope. Not a wish. Not optimism, which is a weather forecast about how things will probably turn out. Peter's hope is anchored in something that already happened: a tomb that was empty, a friend he saw alive again. And he had his own reason to need it. On Easter morning, in Mark's Gospel, the message for the disciples names him in particular: go, tell his disciples and Peter. Then Peter describes what the hope looks toward, an inheritance with three nots. It can't perish. It can't be stained. It can't fade. In Greek all three begin with the same little a-, meaning not. Peter doesn't pretend the present is easy. He says his readers are grieving in various trials for a while, and he compares their faith to gold tested by fire. The hope doesn't remove the fire. It tells you what the fire is for. Then a line to the readers themselves: "Whom having not seen, you love." Peter had seen. They hadn't. He's writing to people who love someone they've never laid eyes on, and he tells them their joy is real anyway.
screen: `LIVELY MEANS LIVING.` · `HOPE, NOT A WEATHER FORECAST.` · `CAN'T PERISH, STAIN OR FADE.` · `WHOM HAVING NOT SEEN, YOU LOVE.` · then, large: `REGENERATED UNTO A LIVELY HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one hope. Sit comfortably and let your breathing settle. Notice what you're carrying right now, the trial, the worry, whatever's heavy. You don't need to fix it. Just let it be there. Then, underneath it, look for one hope. Not a forecast, not a plan. Something you hope for that's bigger than this week: for someone you love, for the world, for yourself. Name it once, quietly. If you pray, you can hold it alongside Peter's living hope, the resurrection. If you don't, just let the hope sit beside the weight, both of them real. The bell holds the time.
Peter. The apostle who denied Christ three times by a fire, and years later opened his letter with a blessing: a living hope born of the resurrection. Today's word.
Your line: gold tested by fire. Today, when the worry comes back, name your hope right after it, out loud if you can. Day six hundred eight.

howItsDone: Readings from the first letter of Peter are heard at Mass during the Easter season, and Catholics count hope as one of the three theological virtues, with faith and charity, anchored in the resurrection of Christ.

fork.setup: you're Peter, the one who denied Jesus three times. years later you write to Christians who are being mocked for their faith. how do you begin?

fork.reveal: after a short greeting, Peter blesses God for a living hope, born of the resurrection. the man who denied Jesus writes first about hope.

original.note: Greek: a living hope (1 Peter 1:3). the Douay-Rheims renders it a lively hope.

trapdoor: what you thought: hope means feeling optimistic about the future.
what it means: a living hope anchored in the resurrection, something already done, not a forecast of what might happen.
what a scholar hears: an inheritance aphthartos, amiantos, amarantos: three 'nots' in a row: imperishable, undefiled, unfading.

notes: Authorship: the script presents the letter as Peter's, following the letter and Catholic tradition; many scholars discuss whether it was written by Peter or in his name (with Silvanus, 5:12). Consider whether a line acknowledging this is needed.
Aphthartos, amiantos, amarantos in 1 Peter 1:4, and amarantos as the source of 'amaranth' (via Greek amarantos, unfading): confirm.
The courtyard fire: Luke 22:55 and John 18:18 place Peter by a fire; Peter wept in Luke 22:62 and Matthew 26:75. Confirm.
1 Peter is read on Sundays of Easter in Year A of the lectionary. Confirm the howItsDone wording.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the hook said the courtyard was 'the last time we saw Peter in the Gospels near a fire', but John 21:9 puts him at a charcoal fire with the risen Jesus afterward; it now simply tells Luke's courtyard scene (and drops 'swearing', which is Matthew and Mark, not Luke); 'the one Jesus came back for' replaced with Mark 16:7 ('tell his disciples and Peter'); cut the amaranth etymology, the superlative 'tenderest lines' and 'almost every Christian since'.
